thread.title: De: Is artificial intelligence really the magic tool for everything?
thread.title_full: De: Is artificial intelligence really the magic tool for everything?

author: Anuska De
title: De: Is artificial intelligence really the magic tool for everything?
text:
If you look around Northwestern’s campus, you might find more than a few people gazing at their laptop screen, chatting with artificial intelligence tools.
From clarifying technical concepts or seeking homework assistance to sorting out their life schedule and sharing mental health statuses, AI provides the desired output to every individual. If you don’t like the reply you receive, just try altering your prompt or even switching the AI model with the plethora of alternative options available in the market until you reach your destination.
Within a short period of time, AI has become an essential, if not necessary, part of the daily routine of many people across all ages. I, at times, feel so overwhelmed by the overuse of AI in my surroundings, that I can’t help but compare its omnipresence to the very Almighty.
With its large presence and transmission to all fields, NU has dedicated a section of its research programs to the growth and development of AI. Having closely observed and partaken in the current style of conducting research, starting from sharing the data-driven problem with AI, then using AI for coding and finally relying on AI to help present the report, I cannot help but compare it to the democratic ideal. Just as democracy is described as “of the people, by the people, for the people,” modern AI-driven research increasingly appears to be “of AI, by AI, for AI.”
AI is helping build itself just like an amoeba, which splits and continues expanding. Every input provided to the model acts like a catalyst. Human beings have merely been reduced to a training data generating mechanism. If humans resort to artificial intelligence for every obstacle or question in their professional or personal life, the evolution of their own intelligence is dubious.
For instance, in the classroom, student-teacher interactions have always been a major component. Now I see so many students simply clicking photos of portions of whiteboards or slides they need more clarification on and giving it to AI. Validation from AI seems to have become a keynote step before turning in assignments.
I clearly remember the time when AI had not yet erupted, and group discussions fostered not just clarification but also friendships. Teacher-student conversations led to the unleashing of newer topics of mutual interest and relationships that lasted beyond the academic year. Perhaps AI users are unknowingly replacing this crucial part of communication in their life with AI itself.
AI shouldn’t be anti-intelligence, but undeniably its overuse alarms me. In 2024, Nobel Prize in Physics recipients John J. Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton led future generations to ponder how far “human” intelligence can go.
The foundational element of AI research is largely inspired by the functioning of the human brain, hence the name “artificial” intelligence. The instinct, logic and ability to solve problems lies inside your own brain. The debate over whether robots perform better than humans originated in the invention of computers and will continue forever.
Genuine victory in such a debate does not lie in declaring one side as the winner, but in ensuring meaningful participation and critical engagement from both perspectives. Only then can individuals develop a balanced understanding of the issue, both technically and ethically. The moment someone relies on prompts such as “Help me prepare for a debate on the topic themed robots vs. humans,” the essence of the discussion becomes diluted, as the debate may no longer reflect independent thought.
What truly matters is approaching the question of humans versus robots and computers through one’s own reasoning, without being overly influenced by opinions generated by AI tools. This encourages a deeper exploration of the issue from every angle. One person may value the efficiency, precision and scalability of AI, while another may emphasize the importance of human judgment, creativity and emotional intelligence.
However, the real success of the debate is not about proving one side superior to the other. Rather, it is about understanding the strengths, limitations and implications of both sides in a thoughtful and informed manner.
AI may seem to provide you with the most coherent and concise answers, present the popular views on an issue, help debug code, correct grammar and improve fluency of content.
But a true teacher will never solve your problems straightaway like AI does. Rather, they will train and equip you to do it yourself. Creators and innovators have always held a higher stature in society compared to the users themselves. Redundancy is a deliberate choice to curtail individuality, making you easily replaceable. The key to achieving something impactful is thinking naturally rather than being slaves to the machine. Great innovation doesn’t occur instantaneously, it takes months of consistent dedication and patience which only living in the “real” world can train.
Anushka De is a Ph.D. student in the department of statistics and data science. She can be contacted at anushkade2030@u.northwestern.edu .
